Chapter 10: Thriving in the First 90 Days and Beyond
Landing a new job is a huge accomplishment, right? But the real adventure starts when you step into that new role. The first 90 days are packed with both challenges and possibilities—especially if you’re an introvert. This is your window to set up routines, connect with others, and show what you bring to the table—in a way that actually feels good for you.
So, how do you make this transition work for you? It all comes down to being intentional and knowing yourself. Start off by soaking up the culture. Watch how your colleagues interact. Notice which communication styles seem to click, and pay attention to how decisions really get made. Here’s where being an introvert is actually a superpower—your knack for listening and observing helps you tune in to these subtle signals fast.
Let’s talk about some practical steps you can take to settle in and shine:
First, set clear goals. It’s a good idea to sit down with your manager and hash out what’s expected of you, and what your top priorities should be for those first few months.
Next, build relationships—but take it at your own pace. Try setting up some one-on-one chats with teammates or mentors. It’s a relaxed way to learn about their roles, and get a feel for how the team works.
Another tip? Go for some early wins. Look for small projects or tasks where you can use your strengths and make a real impact, even if it’s just in a small way at first.
And don’t forget to schedule downtime. Balancing social time with quieter moments for focused work is key to staying energized and clear-headed.
Here’s a real-world example: If you’re introverted, you might volunteer to organize a project timeline, or put together a summary of a team meeting. These kinds of tasks let you use your skills in planning and communication, while still helping the whole group move forward.
And if you find that open office spaces or back-to-back meetings are draining, it’s okay to speak up. Talk with your manager about what you need—maybe that means flexible hours, or the option to work from home now and then.
As time goes by, you’ll find more ways to expand your influence. Share your insights, mentor someone new, or even lead projects that really excite you. The big idea here is to build a career that’s both sustainable and meaningful—one that lets you use your unique strengths and keeps you growing.
